prisoner.name: Denzel Draughn
prisoner.description: Denzel Draughn was arrested during a Black Lives Matter protest in San Diego on August 28, 2020. Police accused him of pepper-spraying officers; his defense said he acted to protect a protester. He remained jailed into September while supporters challenged his high bail. A jury acquitted him on December 9, 2021. His precise jail-release date is unverified.

cases.charges: Unlawful use of tear gas against peace officers and resisting/use of force against officers
cases.convicted: Acquitted of all charges by jury on December 9, 2021
cases.sentence: No sentence: acquitted. Detained following the August 28, 2020 arrest and still jailed at the September 9 bail hearing. Bail was reduced from $750,000 to $150,000. The later acquittal report confirms he was free, but does not establish the precise day he left jail. Earlier reports list differing charge totals as proceedings developed; no dismissed count is presented as a conviction.

case_research.custody_evidence: Actual pretrial confinement beyond the initial arrest; later acquittal and freedom verified. Acquittal is not used as the jail-release date.

prisoner.name: Taylor Breann Enterline
prisoner.description: Taylor Breann Enterline is a racial-justice protester arrested in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in September 2020 after the police killing of Ricardo MuÃ±oz. She spent three days in pretrial custody. A jury later convicted her of riot and four related offenses but acquitted her of conspiracy. She received probation in 2023, and the judgment was affirmed in 2024. She maintained that her protest was peaceful.

cases.charges: Riot; failure to disperse; obstruction of highways; disorderly conduct; defiant trespass
cases.convicted: Jury conviction January 19, 2023; acquitted of conspiracy to commit riot
cases.sentence: Three years of probation imposed April 4, 2023, with restitution and community service; affirmed May 31, 2024. The qualifying imprisonment was September 2020 pretrial detention, not the probation term. The appellate court rejected her sufficiency and weight challenges; it did not require proof that she personally threw or broke objects.
